question: Why must healthcare resources always be carefully managed and rationed?

options.A: Governments prefer to spend money on education instead of health
options.B: Patients rarely use the medical services provided to them
options.C: Medical equipment is always too expensive to manufacture
options.D: Resources are limited while human healthcare needs are infinite

explanation: You'll see this a lot in practice: money, beds, and staff are finite, but sick patients always need care. That gap means we have to make smart choices! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h1)

question: How does scarcity directly affect your daily life as a nurse on the ward?

options.A: It forces nurses to prioritize care and manage limited supplies efficiently
options.B: It requires nurses to personally fund ward equipment purchases
options.C: It automatically lowers the quality of medications available in pharmacies
options.D: It prevents hospitals from ever admitting emergency trauma patients

explanation: Spot on! Because time and gloves are never endless, great nurses learn to prioritize and manage what they have to keep every patient safe. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h1)

question: What do we mean by the term 'opportunity cost' in health economics?

options.A: The profit a pharmaceutical company makes on a new vaccine
options.B: The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
options.C: The total amount of money a hospital spends on patient medications
options.D: The discount given to patients who pay for medical care in cash

explanation: Think of opportunity cost as what you sacrifice. When you choose to spend your last Naira on transport instead of snacks, the snack is your opportunity cost! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h2)

question: A clinic buys an expensive new lab machine instead of hiring two community health nurses. What is the opportunity cost here?

options.A: The financial cost of maintaining the new laboratory machine
options.B: The total budget allocated to the hospital for the entire year
options.C: The electricity used to power the laboratory equipment daily
options.D: The services and community health work provided by the two nurses

explanation: Exactly. By picking the machine, the clinic gave up the care those two nurses would have delivered to the community. That's the price of the choice! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h2)

question: Why is buying healthcare different from buying regular items like shoes or phones?

options.A: The price of medical care never changes based on economic factors
options.B: Patients can easily treat themselves without professional assistance
options.C: Healthcare items are always distributed by governments for free
options.D: People demand healthcare because they want health, not because it is a source of pleasure

explanation: Nobody wakes up wishing to visit the hospital for fun! We seek care simply to get our health back and function well. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h3)

question: What does 'information asymmetry' mean in the healthcare setting?

options.A: Patients understand treatment options better than hospital administrators
options.B: Medical prices are published openly for everyone in the community to see
options.C: Doctors possess much more medical knowledge than their patients
options.D: Health insurance companies have access to all patient medical records

explanation: It just means an imbalance: the doctor or nurse has years of professional training, while the patient often relies entirely on our guidance to understand what's wrong. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h3)

question: In health economics, what does 'supply' actually refer to?

options.A: The total number of patients waiting to be seen in an emergency department
options.B: The quantity of healthcare goods and services providers are willing and able to offer
options.C: The government budget allocated for public health campaigns each year
options.D: The amount of money patients are willing to pay for prescription drugs

explanation: Supply is simply what hospitals, clinics, and health workers make available for people to use—like hospital beds, drugs, and clinic hours. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which of these would most directly lower the supply of healthcare services in a rural health clinic?

options.A: A shortage of trained nurses and doctors willing to work in the area
options.B: Lower prices charged by local pharmacies for basic antibiotics
options.C: An increase in the number of patients seeking routine health checkups
options.D: Higher patient satisfaction scores reported after clinic visits

explanation: Spot on! If health workers aren't there, the clinic simply cannot provide care, no matter how many patients show up. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h4)

question: What does 'market equilibrium' mean in simple terms?

options.A: Consumers buy everything available without worrying about their budgets
options.B: The quantity demanded by consumers equals the quantity supplied by producers
options.C: The government sets a fixed price for all goods sold in the country
options.D: Producers make maximum profit by charging the highest possible prices

explanation: Equilibrium is the sweet spot where what buyers want matches exactly what sellers are putting out. Everything balances out! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why does the healthcare market struggle to act like a normal open market?

options.A: Doctors and hospitals never charge money for emergency life-saving procedures
options.B: The supply of doctors always matches the exact number of sick people
options.C: Government regulations, insurance systems, and emergencies constantly interfere with free market forces
options.D: Patients always know the exact cost of their medical treatments before admission

explanation: Healthcare isn't like buying shoes. Emergencies happen without warning, and governments step in because health is a basic human right, not just a commodity. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is an economic 'externality'?

options.A: An effect of a transaction that impacts third parties not directly involved
options.B: An unexpected side effect experienced after taking a new prescription pill
options.C: The tax paid by pharmaceutical companies on imported medical drugs
options.D: The total profit earned by a private hospital from foreign patients

explanation: An externality is a spillover effect. It happens when something you do affects other people around you who didn't take part in the original action. [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h6)

question: Why do public health campaigns often provide free childhood immunizations?

options.A: Pharmaceutical companies give away extra vaccines to charity for free
options.B: Vaccines create positive externalities by building community herd immunity
options.C: Infectious diseases never spread unless children are in school
options.D: Parents refuse to take their children to private clinics for shots

explanation: Brilliant! When you immunize a child, you don't just protect them—you shield the whole community by stopping the spread of disease. That's a powerful positive externality! [learn more](GST322_U1_T1#GST322_U1_T1_h6)
